name: Crouton
subcategory: family organization, recipes and household inventory
tagline: Organize recipes, meal plans, timers, and a grocery list locally

tiers.name: Basic
tiers.limits: Store and organize up to 5 recipes; meal planning, grocery lists, cooking mode, timers, iCloud sync, conversion, scaling, guided weighing.

tiers.name: Crouton Plus
tiers.limits: Unlimited recipes and family sharing; no AI import, enhanced scanning or recipe feeds.

tiers.name: Discover Monthly
tiers.limits: Unlimited recipes, family sharing, AI recipe import from photos/text, enhanced cookbook scanning, recipe feeds/RSS.

tiers.name: Discover Yearly
tiers.limits: Unlimited recipes, family sharing, AI recipe import from photos/text, enhanced cookbook scanning, recipe feeds/RSS.

pricing.freeTierCaps: $0; store and organize up to 5 recipes; core meal planning/grocery/cooking/timer/sync features included.
pricing.billingTerms: free + one-time Plus + monthly/yearly Discover subscription
pricing.hiddenCosts: AI import, enhanced scanning and recipe feeds require Discover; unlimited recipe storage/family sharing require Plus or Discover.

verdictSummary: The core loop is small enough for a capable coding agent to produce a useful local version in one sitting. For Crouton, organize recipes, meal plans, timers, and a grocery list locally. The hard boundary is native apple apps, recipe capture, household sharing, sync, and cooking polish, plus sync, integrations, and household adoption.
coreLoopDIY: Organize recipes, meal plans, timers, and a grocery list locally, share or print a simple plan, and keep the data portable and owner-controlled.
whatYouLose: native Apple apps, recipe capture, household sharing, sync, and cooking polish
ongoingBurden: multi-user conflicts, reminders, notifications, imports, barcode data, smart-home APIs, backups, and long-term maintenance
whyPeopleStillPay: People still pay for Crouton because household apps survive when every family member actually uses them and the data stays current across devices. The recurring cost buys multi-user conflicts, reminders, notifications, imports, barcode data, smart-home APIs, backups, and long-term maintenance, not just the visible interface.

priorArt.name: Mealie
priorArt.desc: Active open-source recipe manager and meal planner for households.

rejectedAlternatives.name: KitchenOwl
rejectedAlternatives.desc: Covers recipes, plans, and groceries but not the timer requirement, and still calls itself Public Alpha.

rejectedAlternatives.name: Mealie
rejectedAlternatives.desc: A strong recipe and meal-planning server; cooking timers remain a requested feature, not a finished one.

rejectedAlternatives.name: RecipeSage
rejectedAlternatives.desc: Recipes, meal plans, and groceries are excellent; integrated cooking timers are not there.

notes: Editorial comparison targets the Crouton Plus plan and a single-household organizer DIY substitute. Recheck price before merge.
prompt:
Build a personal replacement for Crouton in an empty repository.
Use Next.js 15, TypeScript, SQLite, Drizzle ORM, and a local-first PWA; do not offer alternative stacks.
The core loop is: organize recipes, meal plans, timers, and a grocery list locally, share or print a simple plan, and keep the data portable and owner-controlled.
Make the first run work locally with one documented command.
Store all user data locally by default and make export straightforward.
Put secrets in .env, ship .env.example, and never commit credentials.
Create household members, shared lists, calendar items, recipes or inventory records, and assignments.
Provide fast mobile-first capture with large controls, offline queueing, and conflict-safe sync to one server.
Support recurring chores or events, reminders, completion history, and printable views.
Add CSV or JSON import and export plus photo attachments with clear size limits.
Allow private and shared items and make every change attributable and undoable.
Add backups, household export, member removal, and a simple invite code.
Include clear empty, loading, success, and recoverable error states.
Add input validation, safe filenames, and graceful handling of unavailable APIs.
Write focused tests for the core transformation and one end-to-end happy path.
Create a README with setup, architecture, permissions, data location, and backup steps.
Do not add accounts, billing, telemetry, analytics, or a hosted control plane.
Deliberately leave out retailer ordering and proprietary product catalogs.
Deliberately leave out broad smart-home integrations.
Deliberately leave out large public recipe libraries and polished native mobile clients.
Finish by running the tests and listing the exact commands used.
